summary: Surveys which cryptographic authentication algorithms the routing protocols OSPFv2, IS-IS and RIP support or should support. These protocols have long used cleartext or MD5 authentication, and work was under way to add the SHA family of hashes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers prove who they are to each other with a secret handshake. This note lists which handshakes each type of router can use and which ones are safer.

questions: sha support for routing protocol authentication
subtitle: Cryptographic authentication standards for routing protocols

tldr.problem: Routing protocols like OSPF, IS-IS, and RIP historically used weak authentication mechanisms (cleartext passwords and MD5). As attacks on MD5 became known, the community needed to agree on which cryptographic algorithms implementations should support.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6094 surveyed the existing and proposed authentication algorithms for three major routing protocols and recommends which algorithms implementations should support to ensure interoperability, favoring SHA-based hashing over the deprecated MD5.
tldr.outcome: This informational document guides vendors and operators toward consistent use of stronger authentication algorithms across routing protocol implementations.

today: RFC 6094 is an Informational specification and has not been obsoleted. It provided guidance as the industry transitioned from MD5 to SHA. Most modern router implementations now support SHA-256 or higher for routing protocol authentication, though many networks retain MD5 support for backward compatibility with older equipment.

sections.title: Authentication in Routing
sections.content:
Routing protocols like OSPF, IS-IS, and RIP are the control-plane messages that tell routers how to forward traffic. If an attacker can inject false routing messages, they can redirect traffic to themselves or disrupt the network. To prevent this, routing protocols use authentication to verify that messages come from trusted neighbors.

Traditionally, routing protocols offered three authentication options: no authentication (null), simple cleartext passwords, and cryptographic message authentication codes. Cleartext passwords are useless because anyone on the network can see them. Cryptographic authentication uses a shared secret key to compute a digest that proves knowledge of the key without revealing it. For many years, MD5 was the standard, but research showed practical attacks on MD5's collision resistance. The community began moving toward the SHA family of stronger hash functions.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need to know a neighbor is real before trusting its routing updates. MD5 was the old way to prove it, but it got weak. SHA is the new way, and this document says which SHA version each router type should use.

sections.title: IS-IS Authentication Requirements
sections.content:
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is a link-state routing protocol. RFC 5304 mandated HMAC-MD5 for cryptographic authentication. RFC 5310 later defined a more flexible generic cryptographic authentication scheme that supports any hash function.

RFC 6094 recommends that all IS-IS implementations support RFC 5310's generic scheme, since it allows use of stronger algorithms. For algorithm selection, implementations should support at least one of SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512 in addition to the older MD5, to ensure interoperability while allowing migration away from MD5.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS routers old say MD5, new ones say 'any hash'. The standard should let them pick SHA-256 or another SHA, but still accept MD5 from older routers.

sections.title: OSPF Authentication Requirements
sections.content:
OSPF Version 2 (OSPFv2) offers three authentication schemes: null, cleartext password, and cryptographic (which used Keyed-MD5 in the original RFC 2328). RFC 5709 extended OSPFv2 with support for HMAC-SHA-1, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384, and HMAC-SHA-512.

RFC 6094 advises that implementations must support cryptographic authentication (not null or cleartext, which are insecure). For algorithm choice, RFC 5709 mandates support for HMAC-SHA-256 and makes HMAC-SHA-1 optional. The RFC encourages use of SHA-256 or stronger over MD5 to provide resistance against future attacks on MD5.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF routers should use cryptographic mode and prefer SHA-256. MD5 is old and weak, but some networks still need it for compatibility.

sections.title: RIP Authentication Requirements
sections.content:
RIP Version 2 (RIPv2) originally supported only cleartext authentication. RFC 2082 added Keyed-MD5, and RFC 4822 (which obsoleted RFC 2082) added support for HMAC-SHA-1, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384, and HMAC-SHA-512. IPv6 routing protocols RIPng and OSPFv3 rely on the IPsec Authentication Header and Encapsulating Security Payload for protection, which have their own algorithm requirements.

For RIPv2, implementations must support Keyed-MD5 for backward compatibility but should support RFC 4822 for access to SHA algorithms. As with other protocols, picking at least one mandatory SHA algorithm ensures that implementations can interoperate on stronger authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: RIPv2 had only cleartext, then MD5. Now it can use SHA from RFC 4822. RIPng and OSPFv3 skip this and use IPsec instead.

sections.title: Key Management and Migration
sections.content:
Beyond algorithm choice, RFC 6094 addresses key management. Good security practice requires periodic key changes, so implementations must support changing symmetric keys without losing routing sessions. Some protocols allow multiple active keys during transition to enable in-service key changes where no packets are lost. Operators should plan for this, as the RFC notes that shared keys in production networks are often active for years without rotation.

The document also notes that the choice of preferred algorithm will evolve over time as cryptographic understanding improves. Implementations should be designed so that operators can update algorithm preferences and keys through configuration, preparing for eventual deprecation of weaker algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need to swap in new secret keys without breaking routing. That takes careful design. And someday, when SHA gets weak, we'll want to switch to something stronger.
